facts.fact: An argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false; validity depends only on the argument's form, not on whether the premises are true.
facts.hook: Two friends at a coffee shop argue over a silly syllogism about dragons, and one insists it is valid even though dragons do not exist.

facts.fact: A deductive argument is called sound only when it is valid and all of its premises are actually true, so a sound argument's conclusion must be true.
facts.hook: A debate-club student realizes her opponent's argument is valid but not sound, because one premise is simply false.

facts.fact: Affirming the consequent is a logical fallacy: from 'if P then Q' and 'Q', concluding 'P'. Living in San Diego means living in California, but living in California does not mean living in San Diego.
facts.hook: At dinner, a sibling says 'if it rained the lawn is wet, the lawn is wet, so it rained,' and someone points to the sprinkler.

facts.fact: A conditional statement 'if P then Q' is logically equivalent to its contrapositive, 'if not Q then not P', but not to its converse, 'if Q then P'.
facts.hook: Studying for a logic quiz in the library, a student tests the rule on 'if an object is red, it has color' and sees the converse fail.

facts.fact: A counterfactual conditional describes what would have been true if things had been different, such as 'if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it', and usually implies the 'if' part is false.
facts.hook: After missing the bus, a teen keeps saying what would have happened if he had left five minutes earlier, and a friend notes he can never check it.

facts.fact: Philosopher Stephen Toulmin, in his 1958 book The Uses of Argument, described an argument's backbone as a claim, the grounds or data supporting it, and a warrant explaining why those grounds support the claim.
facts.hook: A student outlining a persuasive essay realizes her evidence is fine but she never wrote the warrant linking it to her claim.

facts.fact: A straw man is the fallacy of attacking a weaker, distorted version of someone's argument instead of the argument they actually made, while acting as if the two are the same.
facts.hook: In a class discussion, a student notices a classmate rebutting a position nobody in the room actually took.

facts.fact: Steelmanning is the practice of restating an opposing argument in its strongest form, even stronger than the other person put it, before responding to it.
facts.hook: Before arguing with her father about curfew, a teen tries to state his reasons better than he did, and the conversation changes.

facts.fact: A necessary condition must hold for something to happen but may not be enough: the sun being above the horizon is necessary for direct sunlight, but not sufficient, since something may cast a shadow.
facts.hook: Two friends argue whether good grades guarantee admission, and one explains the difference between necessary and sufficient.

facts.fact: Europeans long treated 'all swans are white' as certain, until Dutch explorers led by Willem de Vlamingh saw black swans in Western Australia in 1697, showing that many observations cannot prove a general rule.
facts.hook: A student claims a pattern must hold because it always has, and a friend brings up the black swans.

facts.fact: In Peter Wason's 1966 selection task, people must pick which cards to turn over to test an if-then rule; in his study, fewer than 10 percent chose the correct cards in the abstract version.
facts.hook: A psychology class tries the four-card puzzle, and almost everyone forgets to check the card that could disprove the rule.

facts.fact: Modus ponens is the valid argument form 'if P then Q; P; therefore Q', and it is valid no matter what P and Q stand for.
facts.hook: A student replaces the words in a logic problem with nonsense words and discovers the argument still works.

facts.fact: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross introduced the five stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance in her 1969 book On Death and Dying, originally to describe terminally ill patients facing their own death.
facts.hook: A teen who feels none of the stages after her grandfather's death learns the model was first written about dying patients, not mourners.

facts.fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
facts.hook: A grandson worries he is not grieving correctly because he is still going to school and laughing with friends.

facts.fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
facts.hook: A teen feels guilty for enjoying a movie the week after the funeral, until a relative explains that switching back and forth is normal.

facts.fact: The 1996 book Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on.
facts.hook: A granddaughter keeps her grandmother's recipe cards and talks to her while cooking, and wonders if that is okay.

facts.fact: The word 'eulogy' comes from the Greek 'eulogia', meaning praise, built from 'eu', meaning well, and 'logia', meaning words.
facts.hook: Asked to give the eulogy at his grandfather's funeral, a teen looks up what the word means before he starts writing.

facts.fact: Mexico's Day of the Dead is traditionally celebrated on November 1 and 2, when families build ofrendas, or home altars, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who have died.
facts.hook: A family decides what to put on the altar for the grandmother who died this year, starting with her favorite sweet bread.

facts.fact: On Mexico's Day of the Dead, orange marigolds called cempasúchil decorate altars and graves, because their bright color and strong scent are thought to guide the souls of the dead home.
facts.hook: Sent to the market for marigolds before the Day of the Dead, a teen asks her aunt why it has to be those flowers.

facts.fact: In Judaism, the closest relatives of the person who died sit shiva, a mourning period of seven days that begins after the burial; the Hebrew word shiva means seven.
facts.hook: A teen visiting a friend's family during shiva wonders what to say and what to bring.

facts.fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
facts.hook: Spending the summer with relatives in Japan, a teen helps set a lantern on the river for the grandfather she barely knew.

facts.fact: During China's Qingming Festival, which falls on April 4, 5 or 6, families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep and clean them and leave offerings of food.
facts.hook: A grandson goes along to sweep his grandfather's grave for the first time and learns why the family goes every spring.

facts.fact: Anticipatory grief is grief felt before a death that is expected, such as when a loved one is seriously ill; psychiatrist Erich Lindemann described it in the 1940s.
facts.hook: Visiting her grandfather in the hospital, a teen is confused to feel she is already mourning him while he is still alive.

facts.fact: In 2022 prolonged grief disorder was added to the American Psychiatric Association's DSM-5-TR; for adults it can be diagnosed only when intense grief persists at least 12 months after the death.
facts.hook: A teen worried that he is still sad months later learns that long, strong grief alone is not considered a disorder.

facts.fact: The Common Application, which lets US college applicants send one application to many schools, was founded in 1975 with 15 member colleges and now has more than 1,000 members.
facts.hook: Filling out the Common App at the kitchen table, a senior is relieved she does not have to write twenty separate applications.

facts.fact: Early Decision in US college admissions is binding: a student admitted with acceptable financial aid must enroll and withdraw all other applications.
facts.hook: A senior hesitates to apply Early Decision because she has not seen what financial aid other schools would offer.

facts.fact: Early Action in US college admissions gives an early decision but is non-binding, so an admitted student may still choose not to enroll.
facts.hook: A student gets an early acceptance in December and debates whether to stop applying anywhere else.

facts.fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
facts.hook: On a campus tour, a senior hears a guide boast about yield and asks what it means.

facts.fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
facts.hook: Waitlisted at her top choice, a senior must decide whether to pay a deposit elsewhere while she waits.

facts.fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
facts.hook: A student whose family cannot pay much compares which colleges on her list look at finances when deciding.

facts.fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
facts.hook: A senior and her mother sit at the computer late at night working through the FAFSA before a state aid deadline.

facts.fact: Under the FAFSA Simplification Act, the redesigned FAFSA that launched in 2024 cut the form from 108 questions to 36.
facts.hook: An older sibling warns about a long aid form, and the younger one finds it much shorter than expected.

facts.fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
facts.hook: A student applying to British universities struggles to narrow her list of courses down to five.

facts.fact: Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions about why the applicant wants the subject and how they have prepared.
facts.hook: A UK student realizes the essay advice from his older cousin no longer matches the new three-question format.

facts.fact: The SAT switched to a digital, adaptive format in the United States in March 2024: how well a student does on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second.
facts.hook: After a hard second math module, a student panics, until a friend explains that harder questions may mean she did well on the first.

facts.fact: China's national college entrance exam, the gaokao, begins on June 7 each year, and about 13.42 million students took it in 2024.
facts.hook: An exchange student compares waiting for US admission emails with her cousin in China waiting for gaokao scores.

facts.fact: In his 1961 book What Is History?, E. H. Carr described history as 'an unending dialogue between the present and the past'.
facts.hook: At a monument, a teen and grandparent disagree about what it means, and the teen wonders whether both readings can count as history.

facts.fact: In 1824 German historian Leopold von Ranke wrote that his work aimed only to show the past 'as it actually was', rather than to judge it or instruct the present.
facts.hook: Writing a history essay, a student asks whether it is even possible to describe the past without taking a side.

facts.fact: In his 1963 book The Making of the English Working Class, E. P. Thompson said he wanted to rescue ordinary workers from 'the enormous condescension of posterity'.
facts.hook: Researching family history, a teen finds his great-great-grandfather was a mill worker who appears in no history book.

facts.fact: In his 1961 book Griff nach der Weltmacht, German historian Fritz Fischer argued that Imperial Germany deliberately pursued a world war, setting off a long debate known as the Fischer controversy.
facts.hook: Two students in a history class find their textbooks give different answers about who caused the First World War.

facts.fact: German historian Alexander Demandt compiled a list of 210 different explanations that writers have offered for why the Western Roman Empire fell.
facts.hook: A student arguing for one cause of Rome's fall is shown just how many other explanations exist.

facts.fact: The Vindolanda tablets, thin wooden writing tablets first discovered in 1973 at a Roman fort in northern England, record everyday details of army life that official histories left out.
facts.hook: On a computer at home, a teen reads a Roman soldier's letter asking for more socks and realizes most history ignores such things.

facts.fact: One Vindolanda tablet is a birthday party invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, written around 100 CE, with closing lines that are among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman.
facts.hook: A student who thought ancient women left no voice is surprised by a Roman birthday invitation.

facts.fact: An argument from silence draws a conclusion from what a source fails to mention; historians treat it with caution because writers record only what seems important to them.
facts.hook: A grandchild says an event never happened because Grandpa's diary does not mention it, and Grandpa laughs.

facts.fact: Historian Frances Wood argued that Marco Polo may never have reached China, pointing out that his book never mentions tea, foot-binding or the Great Wall.
facts.hook: A student doing a report on Marco Polo finds a book questioning whether his famous journey happened at all.

facts.fact: The ancient Greek historian Thucydides admitted that the speeches in his history of the Peloponnesian War were not word-for-word records, but what he judged each speaker would have needed to say.
facts.hook: A student quoting a famous ancient speech learns the historian himself wrote much of it.

facts.fact: A primary source was produced at the time being studied, such as a letter or diary, while a secondary source, such as a textbook, interprets the past later using primary sources.
facts.hook: Sorting a box of a grandparent's wartime letters, a teen realizes she is holding primary sources.

facts.fact: Historiography is the study of how history has been written, including how historians' interpretations of the same events have changed over time.
facts.hook: A student notices her grandmother's school textbook tells the story of a war very differently from her own.

facts.fact: In common-law countries such as the US, UK and Canada, a contract generally needs an offer, an acceptance and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange.
facts.hook: A teen wonders whether his friend's promise to pay him for tutoring is a real contract.

facts.fact: Under English common law, consideration must have some value but need not be a fair price; courts do not generally judge whether a bargain was a good one.
facts.hook: A teen sells his bike for far less than it is worth and later wonders if he can undo the deal.

facts.fact: In common-law jurisdictions, including most of the US, a contract made by a minor is generally voidable by the minor, with exceptions such as contracts for necessities.
facts.hook: At a gym front desk, a 17-year-old is told he needs a parent's signature on his membership contract.

facts.fact: In the United States, courts generally will not enforce a liability waiver that tries to excuse gross negligence or intentional misconduct, even if the person signed it.
facts.hook: Signing a waiver for a climbing gym, a teen asks what the gym is actually still responsible for.

facts.fact: To indemnify someone is to promise, in a contract, to compensate them for losses they suffer because of certain acts, often written alongside a promise to 'hold harmless'.
facts.hook: Reading a rental form for an event venue, a student stops at the word 'indemnify' and asks what she is agreeing to.

facts.fact: The US ESIGN Act, passed in 2000, says a signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it is in electronic form.
facts.hook: A teen signs a job agreement by clicking on a screen and asks if that really counts as signing.

facts.fact: Under the US Federal Trade Commission's Cooling-Off Rule, buyers can cancel certain sales made at home or at temporary locations until midnight of the third business day after the sale.
facts.hook: A salesperson at a hotel booth talks a teen's parent into a purchase they regret the next morning.

facts.fact: Under the legal rule called contra proferentem, used in many jurisdictions, an ambiguous term in a contract is usually read against the party that wrote it.
facts.hook: A student and a phone company disagree over what an unclear line in the contract means.

facts.fact: A force majeure clause frees the parties from their obligations when an extraordinary event outside their control, such as a natural disaster or war, prevents them from performing.
facts.hook: A concert is canceled after a storm, and a teen reads the ticket terms to see whether she gets a refund.

facts.fact: Informed consent in medicine means a patient agrees to treatment after being told its risks, benefits and alternatives in words they can understand.
facts.hook: At a clinic, a 17-year-old reads a consent form and asks the nurse to explain a risk before signing.

facts.fact: Under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share.
facts.hook: Three friends plan to sign an apartment lease together, and one reads that each could owe the whole rent.

facts.fact: An arbitration clause requires the parties to settle disputes through private arbitration instead of in court, and in the US it is often paired with a waiver of class-action lawsuits.
facts.hook: Scrolling through an app's terms at a computer at home, a teen finds she has agreed not to sue in court.

facts.fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: A teen's pale, steamed chicken disappoints the family, and a grandparent explains why the pan needed to be hotter.

facts.fact: Caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins; table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: Making caramel sauce for dessert, a teen watches the sugar change color and debates when to take it off the heat.

facts.fact: US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
facts.hook: Cooking a family dinner, a teen cuts into a chicken breast to check it, and her dad hands her a thermometer instead.

facts.fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
facts.hook: After a long family cookout, a teen has to decide which leftovers are still safe to save.

facts.fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
facts.hook: A teen starts rinsing chicken in the sink the way a relative always did, and a sibling stops him.

facts.fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
facts.hook: At a mountain campsite, the family's pasta is still hard after the usual cooking time.

facts.fact: Baking soda needs an acid, such as buttermilk or yogurt, to release carbon dioxide, while baking powder already contains both a base and an acid.
facts.hook: A teen swaps baking soda for baking powder in pancakes and they come out flat and bitter.

facts.fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
facts.hook: A first homemade loaf comes out dense and crumbly, and the teen wonders if he kneaded it enough.

facts.fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
facts.hook: A homemade mayonnaise splits into oil and liquid, and a grandparent shows how to rescue it with another yolk.

facts.fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
facts.hook: A teen pulls a roast out right at the target temperature, and it comes out overcooked after resting.

facts.fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
facts.hook: Chopping onions for the family's soup, a teen tears up and her brother teases her for crying.

facts.fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.
facts.hook: Halfway through a recipe, a teen discovers there are no eggs, and learns why cooks set everything out first.

facts.fact: Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle in his 1704 book Opticks, an early version of the color wheel artists use today.
facts.hook: Planning a painting's color scheme at the kitchen table, a teen learns the color wheel began with a physicist.

facts.fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
facts.hook: A teen's gray paint looks warm on one part of her canvas and cool on another, and she wonders why.

facts.fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
facts.hook: Trying to mix a bright color, a teen keeps adding paint until it turns brown.

facts.fact: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
facts.hook: A friend at the community art studio tells a teen to put the horizon a third of the way down, and she asks who made that rule.

facts.fact: Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface.
facts.hook: A teen's drawing of a hallway looks flat until she adds a vanishing point.

facts.fact: Kintsugi is a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold, treating the break as part of the object's history rather than hiding it.
facts.hook: A teen accidentally breaks a grandparent's bowl and decides to repair it so the crack shows.

facts.fact: ISO 216 paper sizes such as A4 have sides in the ratio of 1 to the square root of 2, so cutting a sheet in half gives two sheets of the same shape.
facts.hook: Scaling a poster design at a public library printer, a student notices the A3 and A4 versions match perfectly.

facts.fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
facts.hook: A teen's sketch smudges everywhere, and a friend asks which pencil grade she used.

facts.fact: Pencil 'lead' has never been made of the metal lead; the name comes from the 16th century, when graphite was mistaken for a kind of lead ore.
facts.hook: A younger cousin worries about lead poisoning after chewing a pencil, and a teen explains what is really inside.

facts.fact: Acrylic paint is water-based while wet, but it dries quickly and becomes water-resistant once dry.
facts.hook: A teen leaves her brushes out during a break and finds them stiff with dried acrylic.

facts.fact: Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius, while porcelain is fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius.
facts.hook: At a community art studio, a teen learns why her clay and her friend's must go in different kiln loads.

facts.fact: Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of an image, and artists often draw that space to get a shape's outline right.
facts.hook: Struggling to draw a chair, a teen tries drawing the gaps between its legs instead.

facts.fact: Braking distance is proportional to the square of speed, so doubling a car's speed makes the distance needed to brake about four times as long.
facts.hook: On a first lesson, the instructor asks a learner to guess how much longer it takes to stop at twice the speed.

facts.fact: Under the two-second rule, a driver watches the car ahead pass a fixed point, such as a sign, and checks that at least two seconds pass before reaching that same point.
facts.hook: A nervous learner keeps creeping up behind other cars until the instructor teaches her to count seconds from a lamppost.

facts.fact: The US National Safety Council recommends a following distance of at least three seconds, adding a second for each difficulty such as bad weather or heavy traffic.
facts.hook: A parent supervising practice says three seconds, while the teen's friend swears by two.

facts.fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
facts.hook: On a first lesson, a learner almost changes lanes into a car hidden beside her.

facts.fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
facts.hook: A grandparent tells a learner to pump the brakes, and the instructor explains why that advice is out of date.

facts.fact: In Great Britain, anyone supervising a learner driver must be over 21 and have held a full driving licence for at least 3 years.
facts.hook: A 19-year-old cousin offers to take a learner out for practice, and they find out he is too young to supervise.

facts.fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
facts.hook: A learner choosing lessons at a driving school weighs the easier automatic against the family's manual car.

facts.fact: According to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven.
facts.hook: At the licensing office, a teen reads a poster about crash risk while waiting for her permit test.

facts.fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
facts.hook: A learner forgets her seat belt in the driveway, and the instructor refuses to start the lesson.

facts.fact: A Virginia Tech Transportation Institute study found that drivers texting for six seconds look at their phones for about 4.6 seconds, enough to cover a football field's length at 55 miles per hour.
facts.hook: A learner's phone buzzes during the lesson, and she has to decide whether to glance at it.

facts.fact: Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing, in which new drivers move from a learner's permit to a provisional license with restrictions before a full license.
facts.hook: A teen who just got his permit is disappointed to learn he cannot drive friends around right away.

facts.fact: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road so the car loses traction; easing off the accelerator can let the tires regain grip.
facts.hook: Practicing on a rainy evening, a learner feels the steering go light on a flooded patch of road.

facts.fact: Sociologist Robert K. Merton's 1936 essay 'The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action' listed causes of unintended consequences, including ignorance, error and focusing on immediate interests over long-term ones.
facts.hook: A student council's plan to cut cafeteria waste backfires, and a teacher asks the students why they did not see it coming.

facts.fact: In 1902, French colonial authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people began cutting off tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew.
facts.hook: At the dinner table, a teen proposes paying her brother per chore, and her mother tells the rat-tail story.

facts.fact: The doctrine of double effect, traced to Thomas Aquinas, holds that causing a harm one foresees but does not intend can be permissible when it is a side effect of pursuing a good end.
facts.hook: During a hospital volunteer shift, a teen hears a doctor discuss giving pain relief that might shorten a patient's life.

facts.fact: Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration states that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures.
facts.hook: Debating a new pesticide in class, one student says to wait for proof of harm and another cites the precautionary principle.

facts.fact: In Darley and Latané's 1968 experiment, about 85 percent of people who thought they alone heard someone having a seizure helped, but only about 31 percent did when they thought four others heard it.
facts.hook: At a coffee shop, a customer collapses and everyone looks around waiting for someone else to act.

facts.fact: Risk compensation is the tendency of people to behave less carefully when a safety measure makes them feel protected, so the measure can deliver less benefit than predicted.
facts.hook: A friend who just got a new helmet starts riding his bike much faster down the hill.

facts.fact: A Pareto improvement, named after economist Vilfredo Pareto, is a change that makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off.
facts.hook: Planning how to split a shared car between siblings, a teen looks for a schedule nobody loses under.

facts.fact: In his 1979 book The Imperative of Responsibility, Hans Jonas proposed the rule: 'Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life.'
facts.hook: Arguing about a new technology at school, a student asks who speaks for people not yet born.

facts.fact: In his Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle described each virtue as a mean between two extremes; courage, for example, lies between cowardice and recklessness.
facts.hook: A teen wonders whether confronting a friend in front of everyone was brave or just reckless.

facts.fact: R. Edward Freeman's 1984 book Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach argued that businesses should consider everyone affected by their decisions, not only their owners.
facts.hook: At a part-time job, a teen sees a schedule change that helps the store but hurts workers who take the bus.

facts.fact: Aristotle held that people are responsible for actions done voluntarily, and that actions done under force or through ignorance of the circumstances can be involuntary.
facts.hook: A teen who unknowingly passed on a false rumor wonders how much of the blame is hers.

facts.fact: Many ethicists distinguish doing harm from allowing harm, and most people judge causing a harm as worse than failing to prevent an equal harm, though some philosophers reject the distinction.
facts.hook: At the dinner table, a family argues whether not warning a neighbor is as bad as causing the problem.

facts.fact: The 2018 Gender Shades study by Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru found commercial facial analysis systems had error rates up to 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women but under 1 percent for lighter-skinned men.
facts.hook: A photo app keeps failing to recognize a teen's face while it works instantly for her friend.

facts.fact: A 2016 ProPublica investigation found that the COMPAS risk tool misclassified Black defendants who did not reoffend as high risk at about twice the rate of white defendants.
facts.hook: In a class debate, a student argues computers should decide bail because they are neutral.

facts.fact: Researchers have shown that when two groups have different base rates, a risk score generally cannot be both equally accurate for each group and have equal error rates across them.
facts.hook: Designing a fair grading algorithm for a class project, students find every fix breaks another kind of fairness.

facts.fact: A 2019 study led by Ziad Obermeyer found a widely used US health-care algorithm underestimated Black patients' needs because it used past medical spending as a stand-in for how sick patients were.
facts.hook: On a tech company field trip, a student asks how an engineer knows what a data label really measures.

facts.fact: Jeremy Bentham's 1791 panopticon was a prison design with a central tower from which inmates could be watched at any time without knowing whether they were.
facts.hook: A teen notices she behaves differently at work once she learns the security camera might be on.

facts.fact: In his 1975 book Discipline and Punish, Michel Foucault used Bentham's panopticon as a metaphor for how modern institutions control people through the possibility of constant observation.
facts.hook: Students debate whether classroom monitoring software is more like a teacher's glance or a watchtower.

facts.fact: The EU's General Data Protection Regulation took effect on May 25, 2018, and allows fines of up to 20 million euros or 4 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is greater.
facts.hook: A teen wonders why every website suddenly asks about cookies and learns what the rules can cost a company.

facts.fact: The Collingridge dilemma, from David Collingridge's 1980 book, says a technology's effects are hard to predict when it is new, but by the time they are clear it is hard to change.
facts.hook: Friends at a coffee shop argue whether it is too early or too late to set rules for a new app everyone uses.

facts.fact: A 2013 study by Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation.
facts.hook: A teen working a part-time cashier job watches self-checkout machines being installed.

facts.fact: Automation bias is the tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems and to ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct.
facts.hook: A driver follows a GPS instruction onto a closed road despite the warning signs in front of her.

facts.fact: The European Union's AI Act, which entered into force on August 1, 2024, bans some uses of AI outright, including social scoring of people.
facts.hook: Reading about a school that ranks students by online behavior, a teen asks whether that would be legal in Europe.

facts.fact: In June 2013, documents leaked by Edward Snowden revealed that the US National Security Agency was collecting phone records, such as numbers called and call durations, of millions of Verizon customers.
facts.hook: A teen shrugs that she has nothing to hide, and a friend asks whether she would mind a list of everyone she calls.
